newsitem.title: UK: Sterling soars, defying talk of fiscal tightening. [CORRECTED 15:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Sterling soars, defying talk of fiscal tightening. [CORRECTED 15:00 GMT]

text.p: Sterling is soaring in tandem with UK consumers' spirits and traders are in no mood to allow the first Labour budget in nearly two decades to ruin the party.

Expectations that Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will move to curb domestic demand in his July 2 budget have failed to puncture the bullishness that propelled sterling above 2.90 marks for the first time in five years on Monday.
Traders are betting that any fiscal tightening Brown proposes will be too little, too late and that monetary policy will be left to carry the can in the fight against inflation.
"Sterling is going to three against the mark," said Peter von Maydell, currency strategist at UBS Ltd.

"Labour's election promises mean they cannot whack the consumer with 10 billion pounds in taxes, so there is no way the budget can do enough to offset the windfall money consumers are getting," he said. "The economy is looking dynamic and they will have to raise rates, all of which is bullish for sterling."
Sterling/mark surged to 2.9070 Monday, its best showing since July 1992. It was at 2.9025/35 marks at 1230 GMT from 2.8897/02 late Friday in Europe. Cable was at $1.6646/56 from $1.6614/24 Friday.

Evidence of the strength of domestic demand has been piling up in recent weeks, with the consumer and the housing market proving resilient to the two quarter-percentage increases in UK interest rates seen since Labour took office on May 1.

Retail sales leapt 5.3 percent in May from a year earlier, the biggest annual rise since the end of 1988. Meantime, house prices rose an annual 11.0 percent in June, according to the Nationwide, the largest gain since the third quarter of 1989.
This has kept rate-rise prospects alive even though traders have in the past week nudged up their forecasts of how much fiscal policy will be tightened.
"The tightening cycle on rates is not finished yet, budget or no budget," said Juergen Lindemann, senior trader at IBJ.

"They may come out with a restrictive budget which will make the monetary policy committee hold off rates for a bit longer, but potentially we have another half point, if not a full percentage point, of rate rises still to come."
At 6.5 percent, UK base rates already offer a 3.5-percentage-point premium over Germany's securities repurchase rate and a one-percentage point premium over the U.S. target fed funds rate.
Still, September 1998 short sterling is down four basis points at 92.40, implying rates of 7.60 percent by the end of the third quarter of that year.
(Corrects to make clear contract involved is for September 1998, not September 1997).
Sterling is also expected to be bolstered against the mark as long as expectations persist that the planned single European currency will not be as strong or as stable as the mark.

Such speculation was fanned after Germany's Ifo research institute said Monday it expects European economic and monetary union to start on time, though most countries will not fulfil all the criteria.
Britain's opt-out from the project has led traders to rank sterling alongside the dollar as a safe haven from EMU.

"Sterling/mark is inching its way higher and higher but cable is really struggling to keep up, which suggests that it may have more to do with the fact that EMU is still in the background and weakening the mark," said Lindemann at IBJ.

That said, the mark's relative stability against other European currencies has seen sterling climb against the currencies of most of Britain's main trading partners. The pound's trade-weighted index has risen 20 percent since August 1996 and is now at its highest level in more than six years.
UK exporters such as British Steel have warned that the strength of the pound is eroding their competitiveness and eating into the value of their foreign-currency earnings.
Their complaints have had limited impact on the pound, though, as this has yet to feed through into a significant slump in export data.

"The external accounts will eventually reflect the external accounts, and this will probably end up being the safety valve for the economy, but it is not yet a concern for overseas investors," said Adrian Cunningham, head of economics at Scottish Mutual Assurance in Glasgow.

"UK rates are high, there is a healthy yield pick up, and there is so much bad news elsewhere in the world that even if you don't think sterling can sustain these levels in the long term, in the short- to medium-term it looks like there is more to go."
--Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
